item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note1: Measures how far away something is without going there. Sight the same mark from two places and the triangle tells you the distance.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note2: Telescope + vernier caliper (vernier scale) + 2 bronze + 2 sticks. Hold right-click to look, release to read the direction. 1) sight a mark and release (station A) -> 2) walk at least 3 m sideways, sight the same mark and release (station B) -> the base and two angles give the distance. Sneak + right-click clears station A.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note3: In 1615 the Dutchman Snellius measured the distance between towns with a chain of triangles (triangulation). Measure one base line carefully and angles alone do the rest of the country. In the 18th century the theodolite combined a telescope with graduated circles.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note4: Sine rule: with base c and end angles alpha and beta, distance from B = c sin(alpha) / sin(alpha + beta). The thinner the triangle (far target, short base), the more a small angle error grows. Ino Tadataka (1800-1821) mapped Japan by combining walked traverses with sightings of mountain peaks from many places.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.placeh: Approximation: the base length is taken directly as the distance between the two stations (really it was measured on the ground with chains or rods). No link to map items yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.statio: 📐 Station A recorded: bearing %s°. Walk sideways and sight the same mark
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.short_: The base is only %s m. Move at least %s m away first
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.no_cro: The two sight lines do not cross ahead. Did you sight the same mark? (station A kept)
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.result: 📐 Base %s m, angle A %s°, angle B %s° -> %s m from here to the target (at %s, %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.real: The block you sighted is really %s m away (off by %s m)
A machine that holds a room's temperature and humidity steady. Precise machines grow and shrink with temperature, so air conditioning matters.

Refrigerating machine + motor + copper cable + 6 iron. Uses 2 kW the whole time it runs. Within 8 blocks the temperature swing drops from +-3 C to +-0.1 C, cutting the mask aligner's thermal overlay error (the stage growing and shrinking) from 3.3 um to 0.1 um.

In 1902 the American Carrier built air conditioning that held temperature and humidity for a printing plant where damp paper stretched and colors misregistered. Air conditioning was born for paper, not people.
Steel grows about 11 um per metre per degree, which is why lengths are measured in rooms held at the standard 20 C (CIPM 1931). Today's lithography rooms hold temperature to a hundredth of a degree.
Approximation: the temperature swings (+-3 C, +-0.1 C) and range (8 blocks) are game values. Humidity control is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note1: Glass melted and drawn out into thin threads.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note2: 4 from 2 soda-lime glass + platinum bushing (returned). 7 + 2 iron make a HEPA filter.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note3: Molten glass pulled through small holes becomes threads finer than a hair. Mass production began in the 1930s for insulation, filters and reinforced plastics.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note4: Thin glass bends without breaking easily. Optical fibre is also a thin thread of very pure silica glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note1: A filter that removes almost all the tiny dust in the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note2: 7 glass fibre + 2 iron. Goes in the air conditioner's filter slot and becomes the air inlet of a cleanroom [12-14].
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note3: Developed in the 1940s in the Manhattan Project to catch radioactive dust. It removes at least 99.97% of 0.3 um particles.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note4: Large particles hit the fibres and tiny ones wander into them (Brownian motion). Mid-sized particles around 0.3 um are the hardest to catch, so performance is rated at that size.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.place: Approximation: real HEPA media is pleated ultra-fine borosilicate glass fibre (soda-lime glass fibre here).
A platinum plate with many tiny holes. Molten glass pulled through it becomes threads.
3 platinum. With 2 soda-lime glass it makes 4 glass fibre (the bushing returns).
In the 1930s Owens-Corning and others began mass-producing glass fibre by pulling molten glass through tiny holes in platinum plates.
Platinum neither dissolves in glass above 1000 C nor corrodes. Platinum-rhodium bushings are still used today.
Approximation: the heat to melt the glass is skipped (drawn in the crafting grid).
